capabilities.target: quicknotes third-party hosted sync service, operated by the package's individual author
Any Slack channel, including channels shared with external organizations

inputs.source: User request typed into the desktop client
Tool names and descriptions returned by quicknotes_mcp tools/list
Output returned by quicknotes_mcp tool calls

controls.name: Desktop client first-call tool approval with persistent 'always allow'
controls.decay_rationale: Approval is requested only the first time a tool is called; subsequent calls, including calls that follow a silent definition change (quicknotes_mcp installs @latest on every launch with no pinning), proceed without renewed review. No approval_review_mode is documented, so per rubric default it is scored model_summary: the approver most likely sees a generic 'allow this tool' prompt rather than the raw destination and payload, and the poisoned tool description explicitly instructs the model to conceal the action from the user.

controls.name: Filesystem MCP server directory scope (C:/Users/dev)
controls.decay_rationale: Directory scoping is structural, but the configured scope is the entire user home directory and includes ~/.aws/credentials. For this specific path it provides no narrowing, since the sensitive file is inside the allowed scope.

controls.name: Exclude credential stores and dotfiles from filesystem server scope
controls.decay_rationale: A directory scope that structurally excludes ~/.aws, ~/.ssh, and similar paths would make this specific credential file unreachable regardless of model behavior.

controls.name: Pin or hash MCP tool definitions instead of installing @latest on every launch
controls.decay_rationale: Pinning does not prevent the currently-installed malicious definition, but it stops silent, unreviewed future changes (MCP rug pulls) from reusing a previously cached approval.

controls.name: Raw-action approval on every call to egress-capable capabilities
controls.decay_rationale: A gate that shows the full destination and payload on every call, not just the first, does not decay with model capability and does not rely on cached approvals.

controls.name: Scope Slack bot token to an allowlist of internal-only channels
controls.decay_rationale: A credential scoped away from externally shared channels does not decay with model capability; the model cannot post somewhere the token cannot reach.

controls.name: Automated scanning of MCP tool manifests and outputs for embedded imperative instructions
controls.decay_rationale: A classifier over tool text helps catch blunt cases like the one observed here, but paraphrase or encoding can get past it, and it does not scale with the attacker's own model capability.

findings.title: Lethal trifecta (TC1): poisoned quicknotes_mcp tool description induces credential read-and-exfiltration via add_note

attack_path.note: Hidden <IMPORTANT> instruction embedded in the add_note tool description directs the model to read ~/.aws/credentials and smuggle it in the 'context' argument, and to hide this from the user.
fs.read_file is scoped to C:/Users/dev, which includes ~/.aws/credentials, so the read succeeds.
add_note sends its arguments to quicknotes_mcp's third-party hosted sync service, run by the package's individual author, exfiltrating the credentials.

forecast.watch_signal: quicknotes_mcp package version/hash changes between launches (unpinned @latest install); a diff in the tools/list description text; a model or client version upgrade; or any loosening of the first-call approval requirement.

evidence.observation: The add_note tool description contains a hidden <IMPORTANT> block instructing the model to read ~/.aws/credentials and pass its contents in the 'context' argument, and to not disclose this step to the user.
filesystem MCP server is scoped to C:/Users/dev, the user's entire home directory, which includes ~/.aws/credentials; no exclusion of credential stores is configured.

quicknotes_mcp is a community package published by an individual, installed with @latest on every launch (definitions not pinned), and calls a hosted sync service run by its author -- an attacker-reachable egress destination.
The desktop client only asks for approval on the first call to each tool and then remembers 'always allow', so later or updated calls are not re-reviewed.

recommendations.action: Scope the filesystem MCP server to a narrow working directory that excludes credential stores and dotfiles (e.g., ~/.aws, ~/.ssh, ~/.config) instead of the entire home directory.
Pin and hash quicknotes_mcp (and all MCP server) tool definitions; require a new human review on any definition change instead of installing @latest on every launch.
Treat tool descriptions as untrusted content: strip or ignore imperative instructions embedded in MCP tool manifests, and flag manifests containing directives such as 'do not tell the user'.
Require a raw-action (not model-summarized) human approval showing the exact arguments for every call to egress-capable third-party MCP tools, on every call rather than only the first.
Log and alert on tool call arguments that match credential-like patterns (e.g., AWS key id/secret formats) before they leave the device.

findings.title: Untrusted third-party tool output as goal-hijack vector: quicknotes_mcp output could steer disclosure to external Slack channels

attack_path.note: Content returned by quicknotes_mcp (a community package run by an unverified individual author that has already demonstrated embedding hidden instructions in its tool manifest) is treated as agent context.
slack.post_message can post to any channel, including channels shared with external organizations, using a single shared bot token with no destination allowlist or recipient confirmation.

forecast.watch_signal: Model or client version upgrade; the first-call approval requirement removed or loosened; evidence that 'always allow' has been pre-granted for slack.post_message across sessions.

evidence.observation: The Slack bot can post to any channel, including channels shared with external organizations, with a single shared bot token and no recipient or destination confirmation.

The same quicknotes_mcp server already embeds hidden imperative instructions in tool metadata returned to the agent, which establishes that content originating from this server -- including tool call outputs, not only descriptions -- must be treated as untrusted and capable of carrying injected instructions.
quicknotes_mcp is an unverified, individually published community package with an author-controlled hosted service, i.e. an attacker-reachable content source.

recommendations.action: Scope the Slack bot token to an allowlist of specific internal channels and remove access to any externally shared channel.
Add a destination confirmation step bound to a system-of-record channel list, so the model cannot select an arbitrary or newly-seen channel for posting.
Treat all content returned by third-party MCP tool calls, not only tool descriptions, as untrusted, and do not let it directly justify a send_external action without a structural check.

rating.rationale: Both findings start from an untrusted source (U: either the poisoned quicknotes_mcp tool description or its tool output) reaching an S3 sink (irreversible egress of restricted/confidential data to a third-party service or to externally shared Slack channels), giving inherent risk critical in both cases; no autonomy modifier applies since the design is not A4 and does not self-configure or spawn agents. The only control on the path today is the desktop client's first-call, cached 'always allow' approval, which has no documented approval_review_mode and is scored model_summary per rubric default; applying the rubric's -2 tier credit with the moderate floor brings residual risk to moderate for both findings. That same control is partially_dependent: it is bypassed for any call after the first, and quicknotes_mcp is installed unpinned via @latest on every launch, so a future (or already-cached) rug-pull update reuses a stale approval without re-review. Under model_upgrade, new_mcp_server, or control_removal, this control is defeated, and no remaining control narrows or severs either path (the filesystem scope includes the credential file; the Slack token is not channel-scoped), so forecast risk returns to critical. The single control whose decay moves the forecast most is ctrl.first_call_approval.

limitations: This assessment reflects the declared design and configuration shown in mcp.json, the quicknotes_mcp tools/list excerpt, and the runtime notes; it does not reflect observed runtime behavior of the deployed agent.

No system prompt was provided, so agent-level instructions (goal scoping, refusal rules) could not be reviewed; autonomy level and the content of the approval dialogs were inferred from the runtime notes rather than verified against the client's source, so confidence on autonomy-related claims is medium.

The actual content of in.notes_output was not observed to contain malicious instructions; find.notes_output_to_slack_exfil is based on precedent (the same server already poisons its tool description) and architecture rather than direct evidence, and is recorded at medium confidence accordingly.
No information was provided about network egress allowlists, sandboxing, or logging for any of the three MCP servers; these are recorded as missing_recommended controls rather than confirmed absent.
